name: DNA Sequence Shuffler
seoTitle: DNA Sequence Shuffler Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: Shuffling preserves the exact composition of a sequence — every base, or every dinucleotide — while destroying its order. Free dna sequence shuffler calculato
summary:
Shuffling preserves the exact composition of a sequence — every base, or every dinucleotide — while destroying its order. It returns length, gc content, positions changed and difference from the input, and the panel shows all of them at once.

It is how you build the null model that tells you whether a motif count, a repeat or a codon bias is more than chance. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the DNA Sequence Shuffler
sections.html:
Shuffled sequence has the same base counts: A₁ = A₀, C₁ = C₀, G₁ = G₀, T₁ = T₀. Dinucleotide shuffling also preserves every dinucleotide count

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
A₀, C₀, G₀, T₀base counts in the inputbases
A₁ … T₁base counts in the output; identicalbases
seedstarting value of the pseudo-random generator—

sections.title: How do I use the DNA Sequence Shuffler?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
0% changedIdenticala very short or single-base sequence cannot be shuffled
30 – 70% changedWell shuffledwhat a random permutation normally looks like
100% changedFully displacedpossible for short sequences, unlikely for long ones

  • A mononucleotide shuffle preserves base composition but not dinucleotide composition, so it is the right null for asking whether a motif is over-represented.

  • For CpG or oligo-frequency questions the dinucleotide shuffle is stricter and is the better null, because it keeps the sequence's dinucleotide bias intact.

  • Reproducibility matters: report the seed alongside the shuffled sequence, otherwise nobody can regenerate the control you used.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Shuffling to test a property the shuffle preserves — GC content cannot be tested this way, because it is fixed by construction.
  • Using one shuffle as a null; a proper test needs hundreds and a distribution.
  • Forgetting that a dinucleotide shuffle reproduces mononucleotide composition only approximately for very short sequences.

faq.a: Whether an observed pattern — a motif count, a repeat, a codon bias — is more than the composition alone would produce.
Because genomes have strong dinucleotide biases, notably CpG depletion. A mononucleotide shuffle destroys that and inflates significance.
Pseudo-random from the seed. The same seed always gives the same sequence, which is what you want in a methods section.

faq.q: What does the DNA Sequence Shuffler actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns length, gc content, positions changed and difference from the input. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
